newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Barry Callebaut sees strong Asian chocolate market.
newsitem.headline: Barry Callebaut sees strong Asian chocolate market.

text.p: Asia's chocolate market will grow strongly over the next few years although consumption still lags North America and Western Europe, officials of the Swiss-based Barry Callebaut company said on Thursday.

"We have plenty of growth opportunities in front of us," Frans Callebaut, managing director of the Barry Callebaut Asia Pacific Pte Ltd, told reporters before opening a new chocolate processing plant in Singapore.
The chocolate and compound chocolate coating market in Asia reached about 465,000 tonnes last year against 2.95 million tonnes in Europe and 996,000 tonnes in North America.
"We see more rapid growth from this part of the world, but from a very low base," said Pierre Vermaut, chief executive officer of Barry Callebaut.
The officials said the company, the world's leading cocoa grinder and the second leading chocolate maker, planned to sell more in Japan, China, Hong Kong, Pakistan, India, Australia, New Zealand.
It also planned higher sales in the seven members of ASEAN, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations which groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
The Callebaut officials said the company had to tailor products to widely different markets in Asia.
They said consumers in places like China, Hong Kong and Singapore prefer chocolates that are not too sweet while those in Pakistan or India go for sweet chocolates.
"The palates are slightly different," Frans Callebaut said.
The new Barry Callebaut plant in Singapore, with an initial capacity of 8,000 tonnes, will give the company a presence in the region, the officials said.
It will produce five and 2.5 kg slabs of chocolate for consumers like ice cream houses and confectionary manufacturers.
"The new facility marks an expansion of our global manufacturing capabilities and is our firt major capital investment in the Asia-Pacific," Frans Callebaut said.
Supplies to make its chocolate products will initially be brought in from Belgium, although company officials said they hoped to use cocoa beans from major producers like Indonesia in the future.
